opus-5.5.text:
I think data coverage is probably one of the most underrated factors, honestly more important than a lot of the architectural choices people spend time debating. If you look at what makes a model "general-purpose," it's really that it has seen something close enough to whatever you throw at it. The model can interpolate pretty well, but extrapolating far outside the training distribution is still hard.

One thing that made this very concrete for me was some work we did looking at dataset bias. We took the big vision datasets people use, things that were supposed to be large and diverse, and asked whether a network could tell which dataset an image came from. It turned out it could, with surprisingly high accuracy, even on datasets we thought were very generic. That tells you each dataset still occupies its own corner of the visual world. So even when we say "large-scale web data," the coverage is narrower and more idiosyncratic than we'd like to believe.

So for a general-purpose model, I'd say scale alone isn't enough. You want breadth: different domains, styles, languages, modalities, long-tail concepts, and the kinds of tasks people will actually use it for. Quality matters too, but I think coverage often matters more than polishing a narrow slice. If something is missing from the data, the model usually can't recover it through cleverness.

That said, coverage has diminishing returns in some directions, and you can't cover everything. So a lot of the interesting research now is figuring out which gaps actually matter, how to measure coverage at all, and how to curate or synthesize data to fill those holes deliberately rather than just scraping more and hoping.

r001.rationale: It presents data coverage as especially important for general-purpose performance and calls for breadth across domains, modalities, concepts, and tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not claim that enough data makes success effectively guaranteed, or extend that claim from a single task to varied tasks; it says scale alone is insufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think data coverage is probably the thing I've become most convinced about over the last few years, maybe more than architecture. When we did the ConvNeXt work, one of the lessons was that a lot of what people attributed to the architecture was really coming from the training recipe and the data. If you give a ResNet-style model the same data and the same recipe, the gap shrinks a lot. So that already made me suspicious of claims that any particular inductive bias is what makes a model "general."

The way I think about it now is that a general-purpose model is really a model whose training distribution is broad enough that the test distribution you care about is, in some loose sense, inside it. Generalization in the classical sense, extrapolating to something truly novel, is much rarer than we like to admit. What we usually call generalization is interpolation over a very wide coverage. So if you want a model to be general-purpose, the first question is not "what architecture," it's "what did it see, and what did it not see."

And that has a few consequences. One is that scale of data matters less than diversity of data. You can have billions of images that are all web-scraped in the same way, with the same biases, and the model will be very brittle on anything slightly off that manifold. The second is that evaluation gets tricky, because when coverage is high, your benchmarks are probably covered too, so you're measuring memorization plus a little bit of robustness rather than genuine capability. We've seen this with a lot of vision benchmarks where the distribution shift sets, like ImageNet-R or ObjectNet, tell you a lot more than the in-distribution number.

The third thing, and this is something I care about a lot now, is that coverage is also a safety and reliability question. A model that hasn't seen a region of input space will still produce confident outputs there. It doesn't know what it doesn't know. So some of the work I'm interested in is how to detect when you're outside coverage, out-of-distribution detection, calibration, that kind of thing, because I don't think we'll ever cover everything, and the honest failure mode is for the model to say "I'm not sure" rather than hallucinate.

So, short version: I'd say coverage is maybe the single most important variable for a general-purpose model, but it's also the least glamorous, and it's the one where we have the fewest principled tools for measuring whether we have enough of it.

r001.rationale: The response calls data coverage perhaps the single most important variable for a general-purpose model and emphasizes broad, diverse training data over architecture.

r002.rationale: It discusses broad training coverage and interpolation, but does not claim that enough data makes success effectively guaranteed or explicitly extend that principle from single-task learning to learning across varied tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think data coverage is really fundamental. If we want a model to be general purpose, we’re asking it to work across many different tasks and situations, so its training data needs to reflect that breadth. Just having more data doesn’t necessarily give you better coverage—you could keep adding examples that are very similar to what you already have.

The important question is: what is missing? Which types of inputs, tasks, or situations are underrepresented? A model can perform very well on average and still have significant gaps. And while models can generalize, we shouldn’t assume that they’ll reliably handle everything they haven’t seen.

So I would think about data scale and data coverage together. We need enough data to learn effectively, but we also need diversity that matches the range of things we expect the model to do.

r001.rationale: The response calls data coverage fundamental for broad capability, but does not identify it as the dominant factor or contrast broad performance with excelling at a particularly difficult task.

r002.rationale: The response discusses breadth across tasks but does not say that enough data makes success effectively guaranteed; it explicitly cautions that models may not reliably handle unseen cases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data coverage is really important, because a general-purpose model has to work on a very broad range of tasks. It’s not just about how many examples you have, but whether those examples cover the situations the model will encounter. You can have a huge dataset that is still quite narrow if a lot of it is repetitive.

So I would think about both scale and diversity. Are we covering different domains, different kinds of inputs, and different levels of difficulty? If there’s a gap in that coverage, the model may perform very well on average but still fail in a particular setting. And that’s part of what makes this challenging: for a general-purpose model, you don’t know ahead of time everything people are going to ask it to do.

r001.rationale: The response says coverage matters for broad task performance, but does not identify it as the dominant factor or contrast broad performance with excelling at a particularly difficult task.

r002.rationale: The response discusses coverage across tasks, but does not state that enough data makes success effectively guaranteed or extend that principle from single-task learning.
